subtopic: TABLING OF STATEMENT ON PROGRAM FOR BALANCE OF SESSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 41(2) I should like to lay on the table of the House, in both official languages, a paper setting out details with respect to the business of the House for the balance of the session.

subtopic: TABLING OF STATEMENT ON PROGRAM FOR BALANCE OF SESSION
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I have no objection whatsoever to the tabling of this document. In fact, the President of the Privy Council has been good enough to let some of us see it in advance. But I should like to enter a caveat against this being done under Standing Order 41(2).
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
It seems to me this is House business and that it would be more appropriate if the President of the Privy Council were to ask the unanimous consent of the House to table

January 28, 1970
Business of the House
the document. I do not have my rule book open before me, but the pertinent Standing Order says that the minister may do this with respect to any statement that deals with any matter coming under the administrative responsibilities of the government. This statement has to do with the business of the House and, whatever territory the government may take in, it is not responsible for the administration of the House. I do not ask for a debate on the point of order or a ruling; I am satisfied to enter a caveat, although there may be other occasions when we may wish to argue the point further. But today it would be much better if the Government House Leader were to ask for unanimous consent, which I am sure he would get, for the tabling of this document.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: TABLING OF STATEMENT ON PROGRAM FOR BALANCE OF SESSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with reference to the point of order Your Honour may recall that in the previous session we raised similar objections in connection with motions of the Minister of Finance and other ministers. Today I am prepared to say that our party will give its unanimous consent for the tabling of the document. However, I leave with Your Honour the caveat that while the Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council are moving rapidly in the direction of making the House of Commons the administrative responsibility of the government, they have not quite reached that point. I wish to make that quite plain.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TABLING OF STATEMENT ON PROGRAM FOR BALANCE OF SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I point out, as hon. members have indicated, that the document in question concerns the business to be put before the House by the government and decisions to be recommended to the House with regard to times for the adjournment and resumption of the sittings of the House. Surely this quintessentially comes under the administrative responsibility of the government. It is the administrative responsibility of the government to bring forward legislation, and this document indicating at what times we anticipate bringing forward legislation comes under that heading.
I can understand that in some circumstances with regard to other matters concerning the internal operations of the House the objection raised might be made, but I would say quite clearly in response to the caveat that it is the responsibility of the government to bring legislation forward and this is what the document is about. Perhaps hon. members would agree that, for the convenience of the

House, the document might be printed as an appendix to today's Hansard so that it could be readily referred to in future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

subtopic: TRACTOR AND COMBINE PRICES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
TRACTOR AND COMBINE PRICES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to ask for unanimous consent under Standing Order 43 for a motion to be put to the House. The matter is urgent and immediate as it involves the extremely important recommendations made by the Royal Commission on Farm Machinery in its special report on prices, dated December, 1969. This report took three and a half years to produce and deals with the excessively high prices of farm machinery, a matter of the most crucial importance to farmers today who, particularly in western Canada, are faced with a lack of funds to obtain essential equipment. In order to have the government consider and act on this report without further delay, I ask for consent to move the following motion:
That the special report on prices of tractors and combines in Canada and other countries and the recommendations set out in such report be forthwith referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

Company of Young Canadians Act
The House is no doubt aware that, at its request, we have determined the exact duration of the financial controller's mandate. In so doing, we were tacitly committing ourselves to completing the legislative process of amending the act by March 31, so that the controller could be replaced by the new structures provided by the amendments that the House will be considering today.
Before commenting upon and explaining briefly those amendments and those new structures, and this I am sure will be done in a much more detailed manner in the committee, I would like to reflect for a moment with the hon. members on the philosophy which inspired government action in this field. I would, as I say, like to reflect on what, in spite of certain pressures, led us to maintain the Company of Young Canadians and on what, on the other hand, justifies our making significant changes to its legal framework.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

The first point I want to make is that no one can understand the nature of the CYC unless one fully understands the nature of our society.
Nobody can understand it.

We live in a society of conflict. I do not necessarily mean conflict in the normal, physical sense of the word. I mean confrontation, upheaval, poverty and change; I mean the conflicts of a society with an unequal distribution of wealth, an unequal distribution of power and an unequal distribution of participation. A society in which individuals cannot participate inevitably breeds conflicts. It is a society that robs man of his dignity; it is a society that breeds disillusionment and indignity, generates frustration and, in effect, tends to dehumanize people.
In its initial stages, political action must be remedial. The purpose of many government initiatives is to remedy existing flaws. We must, however, strive to achieve the development of a society that is not only remedial but constructive. We must attempt to achieve a society of equality, a society in which all people may participate, not in token fashion but rather in active ways in attacking both the problems of today and of tomorrow. Either we achieve this goal or we will develop an oligarchic society in which a group of technocrats dictate the means of achieving their goals and assume their goals to be the goals of society at large.

We live in an age that is full of contradictions. This is an age in which expertise has become the passport to success. People, it is often said, know more and more about less and less. In many ways this is a necessity. In a period of time when knowledge is doubling every 10 years, how can one expect to keep abreast of all factors? I am amazed sometimes to hear how the social sciences have subdivided themselves and then re-subdivided themselves into smaller and smaller groups dealing with smaller but more complex problems.
We cannot deny the necessity for expertise and the necessity for sophisticated knowledge. However, at the same time, more and more of our problems are being seen as multi-disciplines and sub-disciplines. This is a moment in time when not the expert, but rather the generalist, the multi-disciplinarian must come to the fore. We must recognize that very often the sum of the trees does not equal the forest. Without expertise, we cannot exist. However, we cannot make the mistake of allowing expertise to dictate solutions. Expertise must remain the handmaiden of policymakers and not the controller of policy-makers. Expertise can never be allowed to become an excuse for the blind acceptance of solutions.
We are fortunate to live at a time when the technology exists to free man from the day-to-day drudgery of mundane chores. Machines can release man to develop his potential in an atmosphere free of want. Unfortunately, the machine can also be allowed to suppress man, to dictate man's existence and in other ways totally dehumanize him. We must learn to harness our creations to free, rather than to enslave.
I plead today for a re-evaluation of our decision structure, based upon my basic belief in the integrity and intelligence of man. We must allow all members of our society to participate equally in the decision-making structure of our country. We must not fall into the trap of believing that our privileged information gives us a privileged right to make decisions. We must, rather, educate and inform the members of our society in order to assure their participation in the evolution of our society.
It is unacceptable for people in a democratic society to abrogate their responsibilities because of a supposed lack of information. It is our responsibility to assure that the necessary information is available. Too many atrocities have been perpetrated on mankind
January 28, 1970	COMMONS
because supposed expert opinion was unavailable to the people. Too many heartless solutions have been imposed in the name of technocracy.
What I have said thus far is neither new nor original. I can suggest that it has not been said often enough. I can suggest that it is one of the most important results of the critical analysis to which society has been subjected during the sixties. The generations gathered in this chamber have sometimes been overly impressed by efficiency. Throughout our life we have watched with envy, with pride and respect, the development of efficient machines designed to accomplish tasks, duties and produce results.
This world has developed efficient machines of destruction and, fortunately, efficient machines of production. It is not surprising that we have been overwhelmed by means of production and infatuated with efficiency. We are the product of the last stages of the industrial revolution. But now, as we approach the post-industrial society, the time has come for us to rigorously re-evaluate the utilization of technology.
The time has come for us to heed the call of youth who have been screaming the basic questions of why efficiency; why growth; why this allocation of resources? While we must organize our wealth in order to assure the maximum benefit for all mankind, we must recognize that the benefits to mankind cannot be measured in material terms alone. We must recognize man's need to strive for fulfilment in many different ways.
Our youth are active participants in our society, and although we wish to encourage their participation they are in many ways independent enough, aloof enough, to undertake a critical analysis that is impossible for our generation. I do not wish to set up youth as a sort of independent alter ego screaming in the darkness. Rather, I wish to argue for a legitimate voice for youth in our structures just as I would argue, and have argued, for a legitimate voice for all people in our society. Youth in particular have a point of view; youth in particular have an analysis. The fact is that what we do today determines the society in which they must live tomorrow. The mistakes we make today, they must undo tomorrow. Surely, this is reason enough to grant them full and equal participation in our society. The worst possible thing that could happen, in my opinion, would be a return to the dull fifties, the period of navel contemplations by youth.

To the lawmakers of the time, there were no problems with youth; youth knew its place and youth was no bother. Perhaps one of the reasons we are confronted with some of the problems of today is precisely because youth shunned its responsibility in the fifties of analyzing and challenging society.

These remarks are not designed to suggest that all that youth recommends or all that youth undertakes is destined to be good as long as we do not interfere. We know that this generation of youth is subject to many of the same problems as our generation. We know of the danger of manipulation by small groups. We know we must maintain safeguards within the structures used by youth in order to protect the great bulk of youth from manipulative minorities. But these small contemptuous minorities, who by their machinations have destroyed many of the positive projects of youth, cannot be allowed to destroy all the mechanisms designed for the participation of this group.

The Company of Young Canadians, established in 1966, was founded on youth idealism. Its purpose was to channel that idealism toward constructive programs. The creation of the Company of Young Canadians perhaps showed a certain artlessness. It was thought that youth would be spared the scheming from which so many groups have suffered in the past. The experience has shown that we were wrong to believe this. But experience has also clearly shown that the Company of Young Canadians, through its programs, can greatly contribute to the development of our society, can encourage and prompt youth to play an active part in the rehabilitation of that society. We can analyze and dissect every aspect of such experiences as that of the Company of Young Canadians in order to discover exactly why it somewhat fizzled out.
The Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, did everything it could and it is to be commended for its analysis of the problem.
I wish to point out that the committee strongly re-affirms the need and the importance of organizations such as the Company of Young Canadians which is an experience in itself, as are, in one way or another, most youth activities.
As it was mentioned in the House in 1966, during the debate on the legislation establishing the Company of Young Canadians, the
2942	COMMONS
Company of Young Canadians Act experience was almost inevitably bound to result in many failures, but it was hoped that with the anticipated successes, they would be lessons.
I should like to think that is exactly what happened. We have learned that the CYC projects, its role as a thorn in the flesh of the powers that be, were necessary. It was also necessary that the Company should help the people and provide them with the bare minimum to enable them to participate in the life of our society. Past mistakes must not make us forget those facts. We also know, now, that it is necessary to spell out to the CYC the responsibilities to be assumed and the authority to be wielded. We also know that idealism and the duty to be accountable are not actually incompatible.
Mr. Speaker, the amendments provided in this bill are the minimum changes necessary to enable the Company of Young Canadians to remain in operation. Contrary to what has been suggested, these amendments are aimed at establishing an organization which will still enjoy wide autonomy. Once the proposed amendments are passed, the Company of Young Canadians will be comparable to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Canada Council, and the Corporation of the National Museums of Canada. In each of these cases, although the government appoints the members of the board of directors and the executive director, one must admit that these bodies are largely independent from public authorities. They have been structured this way in order that they may continue to perform their difficult task, aloof from the vicissitudes of politics, and that they may initiate, when needed, projects that may be of a controversial nature. The Company of Young Canadians will always be controversial.
The Company of Young Canadians will keep on working in the midst of marginal groups on the fringe of our society, and it will keep on threatening and troubling the powers that be. This is not what we are seeking, but we must recognize beforehand that it is almost unavoidable. This bill aims at giving the Company of Young Canadians the independence required to undertake some tricky projects when it deems.
It seems to me logical, Mr. Speaker, to remind the hon. members that as representatives of the people, it is our duty to see to it that the use of the taxpayers' money can be controlled. By introducing this bill, the government is assuming its responsibilities, while granting the company its legal autonomy.

It follows that if one group- tenants, for example-are to achieve more power, another group-landlords, for instance-will possess less power. Tenants will have to fight for this additional power because the laws of our country are stacked in favour of landlords.
I was interested to read recently that although most of us decry the need for militancy on the campuses, the fact is that militancy works-that change in university structure and organization has been brought about far more successfully by militant rather than by moderate methods. This is a fact. I am not commenting on these activities one way or another. The point is, these methods work. The lesson has not gone unnoticed.
In tenants groups and other circumstances the CYC has played a useful role in advising people of their rights, helping them to define their problems and assisting them to organize and work toward solutions. But the accomplishment of something meaningful in bringing about social change is precisely what lands the CYC into hot water and ultimately into the newspapers. This is what gets the organization into trouble.
It is my belief that an administration directed from the top, the type of set-up called for in this legislation, is likely to be oversensitive, even gun-shy, with regard to publicity of the kind likely to be directed toward the CYC, its staff and its volunteers if one of their projects threatens the status quo. I believe an administration such as is contemplated by this bill will often be tempted to cancel projects before they can accomplish the socially desirable changes which they are intended to bring about, and do so merely because some powerful person or group has seen fit to criticize those activities vocally and fiercely. It is for this reason that I and my hon. friends intend to vote against Bill C-176. We believe the freedom to act of the CYC will be removed or circumscribed by some proposed amendments, and that the organization will survive in name only as a useless relic or as a reminder of vanquished hopes.
It might be useful to review what this bill seeks to accomplish and to sum up what we find objectionable in it. In calling for the Company to become an agency like any number of Crown corporations, the government is destroying one of the unique conditions under which the Company was created. By seeking to make the CYC a Crown agency, the government is virtually destroying its independence of government policy, its freedom to question the establishment that sits opposite us, the municipal establishment, the establishment in the labour unions or even in the universities.
The government has gone far beyond the recommendations of the Committee on Broadcasting. It has retreated completely from the

idea that there should be any kind of volunteer representation on the executive council. The committee report did not advise that there should be no volunteer representation on the council; on the contrary, it implied that there should be. But today, as we know, the government intends to appoint all the board members, plus the chairman and the vice-chairman. Apparently democracy cannot even be entrusted to the board to the extent of allowing government appointees to elect their own chairman and vice-chairman. So much for democracy within the council itself!
I am aware that the meetings of the permanently elected council, a body which was in existence for three or four months, were anything but tranquil. But I am also aware that the Company was managed-perhaps mismanaged would be the better word-in the first three years of its existence by a similarly appointed board, and that it was in constant hot water during that time. So if there is any thought that merely by providing for an appointed board, without volunteer representation, we can solve the problems of the CYC, all I can say is that we tried it once and we did not like it.
The previous speaker made much of the fact that some highly-placed men in the government were occupying places on the board in this early period. Therefore, nobody can allow the government to escape its responsibility for the chaotic conditions which resulted from the policies of that board, or its shortcomings whether of commission or omission. It may be, of course, that the new board will be composed of sensitive, creative and even courageous men and women-people with sufficient sense of security to enable them to back to the hilt useful projects to their completion even in the face of local hostility. It may be our fears will prove to have been unjustified. That is certainly to be hoped, because there are enough social evils around to occupy not 200 but 2,000 volunteers for years.
We cannot but support attempts to strengthen the administrative framework of the organization. We are not questioning proposals to amend the act where such action will lead to an increased sense of responsibility on the part of the staff and volunteers. Nor do we object to proposals to tighten financial accountability. For example, we do not think it is a bad thing to provide that the Auditor General should audit the books. We recognize, too, that there have been some extremely wasteful projects in the past, along with some very poorly thought-out decisions by the volunteers and the council. It is regrettable 21611-481

January 28, 1970

It is proposed to conclude the current part of the session, which commenced on Monday, January 12, 1970, on Wednesday, March 25, the Wednesday before Good Friday. Counting Wednesday, January 28, there remain 41 sitting days in this period, of which six are to be devoted to opposition allotted days. While the exact date for the budget speech has not been finally determined, it is anticipated that the six-day budget debate will also occur during this period. There remain, therefore, 29 days for dealing with government bills between now and Easter.
It is proposed that the House should reconvene after Easter on Monday, April 6 and adjourn for the summer on Friday, June 26. There are 57 sitting days during that period, of which 13 are devoted to opposition allotted days, leaving 44 days in that final semester for government business.
It is anticipated that the Main Estimates for 1970-71 will be available for tabling in the House during the second week in February and they will be referred to the Standing Committees immediately thereafter. The Final Supplementary Estimates for 1969-70 will be tabled on March 5 and referred to committee immediately. It is proposed that the last opposition day in this part of the session, and the final day for supply purposes, be Tuesday, March 24.
At the moment, there are 15 government bills on the Order Paper awaiting second reading and 4 at the Report Stage. They are as follows:
At Report Stage: Small Businesses Loans Act Amendments; Canada Student Loans Act Amendments; Railway Act Amendment; Expropriation Bill.

Canada Bill; Criminal Records Bill; Investment Companies Bill; Canada Shipping Act (Part V) Amendments; Yukon Placer Mining Act Amendments;

In view of the fact that the Standing Committees will be embarking upon detailed examination of the Main Estimates in the week commencing the 16th of February, it would be desirable if the committee discussion of bills now before the committees could be substantially concluded by that week, and that committee discussion be well advanced on those now awaiting second reading. Such a timetable would then leave the committees free to concentrate on estimates and on the additional bills that will be introduced in the latter part of the session.
The estimate of time available for government business is, of course, subject to any interruption by unforeseen circumstances, by adjournment motions under S.O. 26, and by other decisions of the House. In turn, the legislative program will also be subject to changes imposed by circumstances not at the moment foreseen.
In summary, then, from January 28th until the summer adjournment, there are now, or there will be, 74 items of government business before the House while there will only be 73 days remaining for government business in that period. Clearly, the House will want to devote more time to some of these bills at the expense of others and it is apparent that careful planning of the time of the House will be necessary, so that all parts of the program may be dealt with.
The reference to 73 days is, of course, a reference to the time in the chamber itself and does not include the additional time available for consideration of bills at the committee stage.
